sections.overview: This small wild betta is native to peat-swamp forests of Sarawak and West Kalimantan. It belongs to the coccina group, whose members are often red-toned blackwater specialists; unlike the mouthbrooding B. channoides, B. brownorum builds a bubble nest.
sections.identification: Adults reach about 3 cm standard length. The reddish-magenta body bears a conspicuous iridescent green flank spot in both sexes, a useful distinction from similarly red B. coccina; spot size varies among local populations.
sections.habitat: It occupies shaded, shallow peat-swamp pools and sluggish blackwater streams, with leaf litter, submerged roots and very soft, acidic water. These forest wetlands may dry seasonally, leaving fish in damp litter or isolated pools.
sections.diet: It is a small predator of insects and other invertebrates. Stomach examinations of wild fish found arthropods including terrestrial ants and aquatic mites, showing that prey comes from both the water and its surface.
sections.behavior: Like other labyrinth fishes, it can gulp air at the surface using a respiratory labyrinth in addition to its gills. It is territorial and secretive in dense cover; observations of group tolerance vary, so wild behaviour should not be reduced to the reputation of domesticated B. splendens.
sections.reproduction: It is a bubble-nesting species: the male guards a surface nest containing eggs and newly hatched young. Reports of occasional mouthbrooding exist, but the standard species accounts describe bubble nesting, so that unusual observation should not be treated as its established mode.
sections.ecology: Its specialised peat-swamp habitat links it to other blackwater bettas, including B. rutilans and B. coccina, but each has its own range and identification characters. Loss of forest cover changes both the shallow-water structure and the acidic chemistry on which this fish depends.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment published in 2019 classified it as Vulnerable, citing its restricted range and continuing peat-swamp degradation and clearance. This wild status is distinct from the availability of captive-bred fish.
